To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the probability of a predator rejecting prey is dependent on the investment in toxin by other individuals in a population.
the rejection behaviour of predators can lead to destabilization of prey defences.
the investment of prey in defences is not the only determinant of the taste-rejection behaviour by a predator.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of prey defences in a predator–prey interaction and the role of taste-rejection behaviour in the maintenance of prey variability.
the evolutionary stability of prey defences in the face of taste-rejection behaviour by the predators.
understanding the mechanisms that stabilize or destabilize variability in prey defence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
taste rejection behaviour can be an evolutionary stable strategy for both predators and prey.
predators can use taste-rejection behaviour to selectively consume less toxic prey.
predators are capable of discriminating among prey with different levels of defence, but that this is not necessarily a reliable mechanism to maintain variability in prey defensiveness.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the taste rejection of defended food items by predators is not accurate across different contexts and therefore does not necessarily benefit the prey population.

the taste-rejection behaviour by avian predators is not a simple mechanism that stabilizes the investment in defence in a prey population, and that the evolution of toxicity could be driven by a complex interplay between the investment in defence and the investment in taste-rejection behaviour.
predators can learn to avoid defended prey, and the learning process depends on the investment in toxin by other individuals in a population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution and maintenance of prey defences can be more complicated than previously thought.
the evolutionary ecology of chemical defences in prey is complex and that we need to take into account the behaviour of the predator to fully understand how chemical defences can evolve.
the investment in defence is not necessarily an optimal strategy for an individual, and that the investment by other members of a prey population is important in determining the optimal strategy.
